entries.title: Windows verify timeout kills the whole process tree
entries.brief: On Windows the verifytree timeout kills only the shell, not the process tree it started
entries.body:
From run-recovery PR-Gate (2026-10-07): run-recovery gave `verifytree` a 60-minute timeout and kills the process group on Unix.
Still open from #420: on Windows the timeout kills only the shell, not the process tree it started.
The step-level watchdog for a `lyx shed step` that never returns moved into task `driver-context` (2026-10-10).

## Was `proc-child-lifetime`

Status (triage, 2026-10-12): the gate move is done; `lyx gate test` starts its child through `proc.StartTied` (`internal/gatecli/child.go:37`, f5b5218f7).
Left: `internal/proc` still has no `doc.go`, and whether `verifyrun` and `gitexec` should gain the parent-death signal and job object is still open.

Two process-lifetime implementations exist once `gate-test-scope` and `git-robustness` both land: `internal/proc` `ConfigureGroupKill` (process group, group SIGKILL on cancel, shared by `verifyrun` and `gitexec`) and `lyx gate test`'s own child lifetime (process group, group kill on a caught signal, Linux `Pdeathsig`, Windows kill-on-close job object).
The orch kept them apart on 2026-10-10 so the two parallel branches would merge without conflict.

Idea: move the `lyx gate` child-lifetime setup into `internal/proc` beside `ConfigureGroupKill`, so one package owns child-process lifetime, and consider whether `verifyrun` and `gitexec` should gain the parent-death signal and job object as well.

The package also lacks a `doc.go`; its file headers carry the description (PR-Gate review of PR #483).

entries.title: Kick-start packs from tool locations through quarry Enclose
entries.brief: Turn file:line locations from verify failures, lint and audits into member glyphs with quarry enclose, then into a kick-start pack
entries.body:
Operator, 2026-10-08: quarry gains `Enclose`, written as quarry's task `enclose-locations` (in the quarry repo; the operator spawns it).
It maps `file:line` ranges from tool output to the innermost enclosing member glyphs, with the same Symbol data `Resolve` returns, also at a git revision (`quarry enclose [--rev R]`).
Markdown is out of its scope: a `.md` location is a per-item rejection.

Use in Loomyard once it lands, building on the kick-start pack:
this waits for task `plan-glyph-tuning`, which builds the Webster pack behind a config switch, and for its with/without measurement to show the pack helps (operator, 2026-10-11).

- Verify failures (`go test` failure lines, `go vet`, compile errors) give the recovery agent or fixer a pack of the failing members.
- Comment-lint findings and Webster audit findings carry glyphs instead of lines.
- A review finding that cites `path:line` despite the glyph rule is mapped at the reviewed revision, then resolved in the working tree, so the fixer's own edits never shift it.

Glyph↔path conversion stays in quarry; Loomyard never intersects lines with symbol spans itself.

## Quarry's Enclose as delivered (quarry PR #36, 2026-10-08)

- Released in quarry v0.3.0: `(*Repo).Enclose(locs)` and `(*Repo).EncloseAt(rev, locs)`, with `EncloseResult`, `EncloseReasons` and `RenderEncloseJSON`; paths are relative to the repo root, not the cwd, and an unknown rev fails the whole call.
- They take location spellings (`path:N`, `path:N-M`, `path:N:col`), not structs; Loomyard formats tool-output locations into them.
- Rejections carry a closed reason set (`EncloseReasons`), including `unaddressable` for a `.go` file in the repo root or a path containing `#`; Loomyard cites `path:line` for any rejected item.
- A `found` glyph may not Resolve afterwards (an explicitly named gitignored file, a file without a package clause, a path through a symlinked directory; `quarry/enclose.go`). Loomyard treats a Resolve miss after Enclose as "no current span", never as an error, the same as a member the fixer deleted or renamed.
- Loomyard pins quarry v0.2.1; this task bumps `go.mod` to v0.3.0, which has no other breaking change.

entries.title: Spawn audit log: every process lyx starts is recorded and traceable
entries.brief: One recorded launch path and a hub-wide spawn log with owner, argv and resource use, plus a sampler and a summary verb, so a process storm can be traced after a crash
entries.body:
## Seen

On 2026-10-08 the operator's machine froze and needed a hard reset at about 20:12 CEST while four runs were in flight.
`sar` shows about 800 process starts per second between 19:50 and 20:00, about 500 more live processes by 20:10,
and the user slice at its 16 GiB `MemoryHigh` with swap full, so reclaim thrashed (8366 major faults/s, 768 MB/s reads).
Only about 15 claude sessions and 9 subagents started in that window, and nothing in lyx's logs says what else started the processes or which run, strand or command owned them.
The operator has seen an earlier storm of 100+ claude panes in reed, and could not trace that one either.

## Idea

Every process lyx starts goes through one recorded launch path that appends an audit line to a hub-wide spawn log:
time, pid, parent pid, the lyx command and trace id that started it, hub, run slug, strand name, executable and argv,
and on exit the duration, exit status, peak RSS and bytes read and written (from `rusage` and `/proc/<pid>/io`).
This covers tmux servers, sessions and panes, claude launches, git, and `go build`/`go test` in verify gates.
A sampler, such as the reed watchdog, also records per-strand process-tree counts and memory every few seconds,
so the state just before a freeze survives a reboot.
`lyx` gains a read verb that summarises the log by minute, run, strand and executable, so a storm can be traced to its source after the fact.

## Was `logger-file-level`

## Seen

The trace files written for each lyx invocation hold only high-level messages, and `_lyx/config/logger.yaml` sets only retention (`trace_retention_count`, `trace_retention_days`).
The file log has no configurable level, so after the 2026-10-08 crash the traces could not show what lyx's subcommands did.
Activity-ranked pruning also left the per-minute invocation counts incomplete.

## Idea

`logger.yaml` gains a `level` key (error, warn, info, debug) for the file trace, independent of the `-v` console verbosity, with info as the default.
Every engine logs its decisions and external calls at info or debug, so raising the level makes most of what lyx does traceable without a rebuild.
The spawn audit stays always on, whatever the level, because it cannot be turned on after a crash.

entries.title: Lens fan: master pre-reads the cited code before forking, forks get a read budget
entries.brief: Make the lens fan work as designed: the master reads the cited code (and judges nothing) before forking, each fork has a tool-call budget, and Discussion and Plan use their own fans
entries.body:
## Seen

The lens fan's design: the master reviewer reads most of what the round needs first, then forks, so each lens fork inherits that reading through the cache and needs little new reading, which keeps a fork cheap enough for a Sonnet medium reviewer.
The first fanned run (`webster-replan-state`, Discussion rounds 1-4 and Plan round 1) did not work that way; the analysis is in `docs/research/lens-fan-cost-analysis.md`:

- The master forked after reading only the target, instructions and stencil (39-74k context), no code, then told every fork to verify the Decisions' premises against the code.
  In Discussion round 1 the master read 19 code files first, and its forks took 32 turns and 152k fresh tokens; rounds 2-4 took 81-125 fork turns and 435-485k fresh.
- Inheritance through the cache works; cost scales with fork turns, about 3.5-4k fresh tokens per turn.
  32-46% of fork file reads duplicated another fork's.
- Fanned Discussion rounds cost 301-638k fresh against 86-121k for solo Opus rounds; Plan round 1 cost 901k fanned against 202-227k solo.
  The fan raised more MEDIUM and LOW findings, not more BLOCKING ones, and about half of raw fork findings were duplicates across lenses.

The responsible text is `clusterRulesBlock` in `internal/burlerengine/prompt.go`: "After exploring the target fully" never says to read the code the target cites, and "Fetch only what your lens needs" sets no budget.
The `standard` fan also points code lenses at design documents.

## Idea

Revise the fan so it works as designed:

- the master is told every lens of the fan up front, and before it spawns any fork it explores, for each lens, what that lens will need and reads it, so the forks inherit one shared reading instead of each exploring on its own (lyx cannot pick the relevant code itself: Discussion review is exploratory, so the master's judgment chooses what to read);
- the master judges nothing before the fork point: a review written before forking would colour every fork, so the master's own holistic review stays after the forks are spawned;
- each fork is told its context already holds the code, and gets a tool-call budget (about 6) for reading only what is missing; forks spending their budget show in the usage record that the master read too little;
- Discussion-Review and Plan-Review use the `discussion` and `plan` fans instead of `standard`.

Estimate: about 200-250k fresh tokens per round, about 2x a solo Opus round instead of 5-6x.

## Operator decisions (2026-10-10)

- The fan stays off in the hub until this task lands and a fanned run shows the estimate holds.
- Until then Discussion-Review and Plan-Review run solo on `opus[medium]`, and Webster-Review on `sonnet[medium]`.

## Research (fan-lab, 2026-10-10)

A research agent replayed `webster-replan-state` Discussion round 2 standalone (`lyx burler run`) per variant, master and forks `sonnet[medium]`; the full reports are `docs/research/lens-fan-lab-phase0.md` and `lens-fan-lab-phase1.md`.
Variants: A today's text; B a lens-agnostic reading checklist in step 1; C B plus a 6-call fork budget; D C plus a reading manifest the master writes before spawning.

| Run | Fan | Master code pre-reads | Fork tool calls | Review side fresh | Verdict | F1 (BLOCKING) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | discussion | 0 | 2 | 216k | APPROVED | no |
| B | discussion | 2 | 8 | 154k | APPROVED | no |
| C | discussion | 2 | 0 | 133k | APPROVED | no |
| D | discussion | 12 | 1 | 198k | APPROVED | no |
| D | standard | 3 | 1 | 154k | APPROVED | no |
| original round 2 | standard, sonnet[high] | 0 | 135 | 619k | BLOCKING | yes |

Findings:

- Only the manifest (D) makes a Sonnet-medium master pre-read; in A-C it read instruction 2 at once and forked after the board entry and a few pattern files.
- No master judged anything before the spawn, in any variant.
- Only the D runs reproduced round 2's code-grounded MEDIUMs; A-C findings were text-level.
- No run found F1, which needs one hop past the target's citations (the D7 guard on `push` → `Fabric.Commit` → `SpawnDetachedPush`); at medium effort the forks barely read in any variant, so no one made the hop.
- Fork cost is driven by effort, not the budget: the original's 485k fork fresh came from `sonnet[high]` forks told to verify against code.
- A D round costs about 150-200k review side, still 1.5-2x a solo `opus[medium]` round.
- Every fork already inherits instruction 2 and so every lens, since the master reads it before spawning.

Recommendation: adopt D, with a checklist line for callers and spawned processes (untested). Step 1 (`clusterPrereadBlock`, explore file only, cluster rounds only):

```
## Reading for the fork reviewers

This round fans out: in step 2 you spawn fork reviewers, and each fork inherits your context as it stands at the spawn.
Your reading in this step is the forks' reading, so read here what the review will need, once, instead of leaving each fork to read it again.

Before you leave this step, read:

- every file the target names, at the definitions of the symbols it cites;
- for each symbol the target changes, guards or removes: its direct callers and callees, and every path that reaches it from another process, such as a child the code spawns or a command that calls the guarded verb in-process;
- the `pattern/` background file of every PATTERN entry the target names or touches;
- the board entry of the task the target belongs to, through `lyx board get`;
- the failure, restart and resume paths of each change the target makes.

Read definitions and call sites, not whole files: a fork re-reads its inherited context on every turn.
Judge nothing while you read: write no finding, verdict or assessment, not even in a status line or a note to yourself.
A judgement in your context before the spawn colours every fork; your own review starts after the forks are spawned.

End this step with a reading manifest as a plain message: one line per file and symbol you read, grouped by the part of the target it serves.
The manifest names what you read and nothing about what you found.
```

Step 2 (`clusterRulesBlock`), replacing the spawn trigger, the fork boilerplate and the holistic paragraph; the consolidation paragraph is unchanged:

```
This is a cluster round: as soon as step 1's reading is done, spawn ALL of the fork reviewers below in a SINGLE message via the Agent tool with `subagent_type: "fork"`, one per lens listed here — never pass a `name` (named forks silently lose inherited context).

Lenses for this round:

<lenses>

Each fork's prompt is this boilerplate plus that lens's emphasis text, and nothing else: never add a direction to verify against the code or to read files.
Your inherited context already holds the target, the rules and the code the target rests on; review from it.
The reading manifest in your context lists what is already read; check it before any tool call.
You may make at most 6 tool calls, each only for something your lens needs that the manifest lacks, such as a caller or a spawned process one hop beyond it, and never to re-read what your context already shows.
End your final message with one line per tool call you made: what you read and why your context lacked it.
You are READ-ONLY — never Write/Edit/delete any file, never run any git command, never touch the two round output files, and never call the Agent tool yourself (forks cannot nest); return your findings ONLY as your final message, each with a severity, a class, a location, and a one-line summary.

While the forks run, YOU (the handler) do your own HOLISTIC review — architecture, cross-file invariants, PATTERN-fit — from the same context, reading further only where it or a fork's read list shows a gap, and prepare the ground truths and the severity rubric you will judge every finding against.
```

## Confirming run (2026-10-10): parked

The recommended text on the standard fan at `sonnet[high]` aborted at the 300k cap with no review written: review side 354k, $3.19, 288 s active.
Three forks raised F1 through their hop budget, so the pre-read and the hop line work at high effort, but the round is slower than solo `opus[medium]` (225 s, $1.45, found F1) and about twice the price.
Solo `opus[medium]` stays the reviewer; this entry is parked as a note.
Two hand-built packs were then tried on solo `opus[medium]`, one run each:

- A body dump (the bodies of the 35 symbols the target cites, about 20k tokens, in a file read first): 312 s, $1.93 review side, missed the BLOCKING finding.
- A kick-start pack in quarry's `RenderKickstartPack` format (a glyph→span line and a signature line per glyph, 35 glyphs, 5.3 KB), injected into the first prompt with "read all listed spans in parallel, in one turn, before doing anything else": 316 s, $1.94 review side, found the BLOCKING finding (1 BLOCKING / 4 MEDIUM).

The operator doubts the second run applied the kick-start as designed either, and will look at it later.
Plain solo stays faster and cheaper for review on this fixture; the kick-start pack's measured case remains the implementer and the Burler fixer (`kick-start-pack`).

Open if the fan comes back:

- The landing text must say "go straight on to step 2 in the same turn": the master ended its turn after posting the manifest.
- The `discussion` fan has no lens aimed at a guard's callers; `scenarios` is the natural owner if a lens change is wanted.
- Proposal E (not run): lyx extracts the target's citations (paths, backticked symbols) as the manifest's starting list without loading code, leaving the choice of what to read to the master; 22 of the 25 files the original forks needed are cited in the target, the other 3 one hop away.

entries.title: Weaver: a cold-start implementer beside Webster, with model escalation
entries.brief: A second implementer built on Millhouse Builder: a fresh agent per batch with its own model, escalating the model when an agent fails; Webster stays fork-based
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-10-11)

Webster stays fork-based: its implementer and verify-fix forks start at once with Master's context and run on Master's model.
Weaver is a second implementer beside it, built on Millhouse's "Builder" (skill `mill-go`), that runs a cold-start agent per batch, so each agent can take its own model, and escalates the model when an agent fails.

## Seen (research, 2026-10-11)

- Webster spawns one cold agent today: the recovery strand.
  When a fork reports `stuck` or writes no report twice, Master runs `lyx webster recover-batch` (`contracts/stencils/webster/webster-template-master.md`), which starts a fresh shuttle/reed strand with a full cold-start prompt (`internal/websterengine/recoverbatch.go`).
  Its model is `webster.yaml` `recovery` (default `opus[high]`), against `master` at `sonnet[medium]`; that is Webster's only model escalation, and a batch gets at most two recoveries.
- Builder (`plugins/mill/skills/mill-go-base/SKILL.md` in the Millhouse worktree) is a lean orchestrator that never reads cards or diffs.
  Per batch it starts a fresh, non-fork agent with a model from config (`roles.implementer.model`), and the agent reads only its batch file and the overview's Shared Decisions.
  It has no automatic model escalation: a stuck batch gets one fresh retry on the same tier, then a plan edit with a `## Prior failure` note, then a question to the parent.
- Millhouse's cold starts were slow: each agent read much background and loaded its tools before it began work.
  Likely further costs visible in the skill: a review loop per batch, finalize replaying every batch's verify in turn, and a state commit on every status change.

## Shape

Weaver is, in effect, Webster's recovery strand used as the normal path.

- From Webster: the Go bracket verbs (begin-batch, record-batch, recover-batch), the report contract and classification, suspect paths, partition and sequencing, the plan-level verify gate and failure ladder, the shuttle/reed spawn path, and `RenderRecoveryPrompt` with `uncommitted_paths` and the failure digest.
- From Builder: a cold, scoped agent per batch that reads only its cards and Shared Decisions, a model and effort per role per spawn, and a one-shot self-resolve before halting.
- New in neither: an escalation ladder per failed attempt, for example `sonnet` → `opus` → `opus[high]`, set in config.
- Open: how to keep cold-start cost down (a kick-start pack per batch, see `kick-start-pack`), and how a run chooses Weaver over Webster (recipe row or config).

## Idea: Weaver as a Shed run (operator, 2026-10-11)

Loom's driver now does little: most of a loom run is driven mechanically, and the driver acts only when something goes wrong.
Weaver gets the same split: a Weaver run is a Shed-like run in which each batch is a producer, and a Master Weaver drives it the way a driver drives loom, stepping in only when a batch fails.

Open against the code:
- A Shed recipe's rows are fixed, while a plan's batch count is not: either the recipe is generated from the plan, or one batch producer loops over the batch index, as the Burler round loops over rounds.
- The escalation ladder could be Shed rows: a batch's `OnStuck` points at the same batch on the next model tier, and the last tier's `OnStuck` escalates to Master Weaver.
- Whether Master Weaver is an LLM at all on the happy path, or only the escalation target, as the hub orchestrator is for loom.

## Idea: batches formed as the run goes (operator, 2026-10-11)

Batches are not fixed up front.
The run starts from the plan's linear card list, and a batchifier forms the first batches: the cards that can be spawned right now.
Batches, or single cards, whose glyphs do not overlap are spawned in parallel, each in its own worktree.
Each time a batch finishes, the batchifier runs again over the remaining cards and forms the next batch or batches.
The plan is updated as the run goes, since an implementer may have to deviate from it, and the next batchifier pass reads the updated plan.

Open against the code:
- This answers the fixed-rows question above: the run is a frontier of ready batches, not a fixed row list.
  The recipe can still be fixed if the batches are data, not rows: a Batchify row forms the frontier, a Batch-Run row runs it and loops back to Batchify while cards remain, then the run goes on to the plan-level verify, the way the Burler round loops over rounds.
  New for Shed: one row that runs several spawns in parallel and finishes when all of them have.
- Parallel worktrees need a merge back into the task branch after each batch; glyph disjointness rules out textual conflicts but not semantic ones, so the verify gate runs on the merged result.
- Who writes an implementer's deviation into the plan (the implementer through its report, Go from the report, or Master Weaver), and how the batchifier tells a deviated card's new glyphs from its planned ones.
- What the existing batcher module (`batcher` config) and Webster's partition and sequencing already give a batchifier.

## Was `webster-parallel-execution`

From `manifest/roadmap.md` Someday.
Give each DAG-independent group its own `fabric`-spawned worktree, so concurrent cards stop sharing one git index.
A speed optimization over an already-correct sequential system.
The loom plan spec and `internal/websterengine`'s package documentation describe the sequential model it would extend.

## Design

> **Status: parked, not rejected — one shape was rejected, a second is open.** What two explorations rejected is *concurrent forks inside one working tree*, which race on a single shared git index; the 2026-08-20 worktree-per-group shape below does not share that index and is not covered by that rejection. Read past this banner before concluding the idea is dead — the earlier wording said "rejected for now both times" and, until the 2026-08-29 designs audit, sent readers away before the open shape, the measured case study, and the decision gate.
> Still parked, though one of its original three reasons has since fallen: the **Adopt quarry's glyph alphabet as the plan alphabet** item shipped (`go.mod` now requires `github.com/Knatte18/quarry`), so the DAG source this doc used to wait on exists. What still parks it: it is a speed optimization over an already-correct sequential system, and webster's landed card-list rewrite (`internal/websterengine`) should get real running mileage first. Reopen it on the measured evidence the Decision gate section names, never on estimate.
> Per the documentation lifecycle, if this is ever picked up the durable parts fold into `internal/websterengine`'s package doc and this file is deleted; if abandoned, this file is simply deleted.

## Why it's parked

loom-plan-spec.md is deliberately a flat, sequential card list with **no DAG wired into scheduling**.
Running cards as *parallel* forks would require reintroducing a DAG and worktree isolation, which reopens exactly the problem sequential execution avoids: git's index/staging area is a single shared file per working tree, so two forks concurrently committing — even to fully disjoint files — race on the same lock.
Current (2026) ecosystem guidance treats worktree isolation as effectively required for concurrent subagents on the same repo.
A declared-disjoint card pair that turns out (via deviation) to actually overlap is a **live corruption risk** in a concurrent-no-worktree model, not just a bookkeeping problem to fix after the fact as it is sequentially;
quarry would also see other forks' uncommitted, potentially syntactically-broken in-flight edits while serving a concurrent fork's query, since there's no filesystem isolation between them.

**A possible middle ground, if revisited:** let forks edit concurrently (the LLM-thinking-dominated part) but serialize the actual `git add`+commit+verify step through a mutex in webster's Go orchestration ("edit in parallel, land sequentially").
Even this requires *strictly enforced* file-disjointness (not just DAG-edge-absence) to be safe.
Not built.

## A possible unblocking shape (2026-08-20)

A structural alternative to the rejected concurrent-forks-in-one-tree shape above: each DAG-independent group (a batch, possibly one card) gets its own `fabric`-spawned worktree — genuinely its own git index/HEAD, which is what the rejected shape lacked — running the existing `Preflight → Webster → Finalize` row set unchanged, with `Webster`'s `Geometry.PlanDir` (already told, not derived) pointed at the source plan and a new batch-filter selecting the one group to run.
Merge-back reuses `fabric`'s existing merge machinery, not new infrastructure, and a group's completion gates on a build+test of the *merged* result rather than of the group's own worktree in isolation.
The ready set recomputes wave to wave rather than being precomputed upfront, so a group that turns out to depend on another's output is simply not ready yet instead of being mis-scheduled.

This shape is what makes the rejection at the top of this doc specific rather than general: that rejection was about concurrent forks sharing one checkout's git index, which worktree-per-group does not do.

Grouping granularity (one card vs. several) is orthogonal to safety — the original rejection above conflated it with the working-tree-sharing hazard, but genuine worktree-per-lane isolation is what actually matters.
Not yet a plan: the DAG source exists now that the **Adopt quarry's glyph alphabet as the plan alphabet** item has shipped,
but it still needs a writeup reconciling this with the still-open questions elsewhere in this doc (typical-plan wave-width evidence, the batchifier/planner change needed to emit groups).

The per-lane mechanics have since shipped elsewhere: batten's recipe (create, seed, run, teardown as ordinary producers) and its run-id addressing carry N concurrent lane runs side by side, so a lane is a batten-style run whose child seed names a webster-lane recipe — none of that machinery is this item's to build.
What remains genuinely webster's: the wave scheduler (event-driven, recomputing the ready set on each lane's merge-back — never a continuously maintained DAG), the plan group-filter, and a non-forking webster variant.
That last one is the real structural change: today's webster runs forks inside the Master session's own context, which binds execution to one session in one worktree;
a lane needs agents spawned into the lane worktree's own reed session instead, scoped to just that lane's group.

## The case study (from an earlier, more detailed design draft, `websterv2.md`, now retired)

A card-level dependency analysis of the 42-card plan that built webster v1 overturned the naive "linear chain" assumption:

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Cards | 42 |
| Batches (sequential) | 9 |
| True card-DAG depth (critical path) | 7 |
| Peak wave width | 10 |
| Cards off the critical path | 83% (35 of 42) |
| Wave widths (1→7) | 10, 9, 7, 7, 6, 2, 1 |

- **The batch DAG over-constrains.**
  Sequential batching's own dependency declarations were largely spurious at card granularity — ~26 cards (waves 1–3) could have run as three parallel waves instead of spread across four sequential batches.
- **File-conflicts barely bind** when the plan is create-then-extend — nearly every file-conflict pair is already dependency-ordered into different waves.
- **The tail is the real ceiling, not dependencies** — a hard funnel near the end of a plan (e.g. final registration → sandbox validation) crashes wave widths regardless of fork budget;
  speedup is front-loaded.
- **Honest speedup estimate: ~2–3× wall-clock**, discounted from a naively-computed 3–5× because a wave's wall-clock is its *slowest* card,
  and the heaviest implementation cards tend to sit on the critical path.
  Two caveats push it down further: semantic edges were *inferred* from card descriptions (real edit-time dependencies only add edges and shrink waves), and 42 cards is an atypically large plan — a routine 5–10-card task has little fan-out headroom and would show a speedup near 1×, dominated by warm-context, not parallelism.

## Decision gate, if ever revisited

Run the card-DAG width analysis across several *real* completed plans, weighted for **typical** task size, not this one outlier.
Wide (fat waves, short critical path, low file-conflict) → an executor might pay off.
Narrow (long critical path, most cards chained, or simply few cards) → parallelism won't materialize;
sequential is the complete correct design, not just the MVP.

## The separable, cheap win already taken

A planner that emits true card dependencies (`depends-on`) instead of an over-constrained batch line recovers most of the *width* insight with **no worktrees and no concurrent execution** — this is exactly what loom-plan-spec.md already does.
Only the *executor that actually runs the width* (this entry) remains parked.

## Relationship to quarry (Part B of the retired draft)

The retired `websterv2.md` draft also had a Part B — structured impact lookup via `go/packages`/`gopls` (find-all-references as a Go verb instead of LLM-driven grep).
That idea is superseded, not lost: it's the direct ancestor of [quarry](https://github.com/Knatte18/quarry), which generalizes it to a multi-language, daemon-based design.

## Related

- `internal/websterengine`'s package documentation — the sequential model this would extend.
- loom-plan-spec.md — already captures the cheap win (`depends-on`).
- [quarry](https://github.com/Knatte18/quarry) — Part B's successor.

entries.title: Discussion premises cite the glyph they rest on; the gate resolves them
entries.body:
## Seen (Discussion bench, 2026-10-11)

Across the Discussion bench arms, most reference findings a draft repeated were reading errors: the code said otherwise and neither the writer nor any twill fork opened it (`classifyDeadlineExpiry`, `contractFileStatus`, `ownTrackedPaths`, go/build's GOOS rules).
Twill opus[medium] missed 4 reference findings, 3 of them reading errors; solo opus[high] missed 7, 5 of them reading errors.
Twill forks inherit the writer's reading, so they share its gaps.
No role is made to read, and nothing checks that a stated premise rests on code someone opened.

## Idea

- Every factual premise in the decision record about today's code names the symbol it rests on, as a glyph.
- The Discussion gate (`lyx loom validate-discussion`) resolves each named glyph with `lyx quarry resolve` and flags a premise with no glyph or with one that does not resolve.
- Reading cannot be forced, but a cited premise is checkable, and a premise like "`rusageStats` is split into per-OS files" fails when the cited files do not exist.

## Open

- Which sections of the record count as premises, so the rule does not reach design text.
- Whether the gate refuses or only warns.

## Operator decision (2026-10-15)

The Discussion writer does prose exploration and does not use quarry or glyphs; glyphs come in only at Plan.
So the idea above, glyph cites in the decision record resolved by the Discussion gate, conflicts with that decision as written.
What stays open is the finding itself: Discussion premises about today's code rest on reading nobody checks.

entries.title: Split the orch into a run driver and a conversational orch
entries.brief: One agent drives runs and takes escalations; the operator talks to the other, which discusses problems and updates the board.
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-11)

The operator follows the orch from the phone through Remote Control, but so much comes in to the orch (batten notices, parent-review requests, escalations, PR-Gate reviews, landing routines) that the conversation is hard to follow.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-11)

Split the hub orchestrator into two agents:

1. The run driver, the repo's upper driver: it reads the board, starts batten runs, and takes the escalated questions (parent reviews, review escalations, PR-Gate, landings).
   The operator can talk to it, but should not need to.
2. The conversational orch: the agent the operator talks to.
   It discusses problems with the operator and updates the board.

## Open

- How a question the run driver cannot settle reaches the operator: through the conversational orch, or as a notice of its own.
  The operator can keep both agents on Remote Control and gets a notification from the run driver when it needs input (operator, 2026-10-11).
- Who writes what on the board: the run driver only claims, sets statuses and prunes, while scope edits and notes stay with the conversational orch, or both write freely.
- How an operator decision reaches the run driver (start this bundle, change a hub config), and how the run driver learns the operator's settled decisions it needs at parent review.
- How much of the run driver is an LLM at all: most of the run loop is mechanical, as loom's driver now is; see `orch-owns-the-loop`.
  Starting a batten run on each ready board task (kind task, `depends_on` cleared, not claimed) needs no LLM (operator, 2026-10-11); nor does the landing routine.
  What the orch adds by hand today would need a home: per-task loom settings such as `review_max_bounces: 2` for a small task (a board field), and a cap on concurrent runs.
- `runs-overview` and `orch-token-spend` touch the same split.

## Idea: the run driver as a Go program (operator, 2026-10-12)

Perhaps the part split out of the orch is a Go-driven program: Go handles most of it on its own (starting ready tasks with their run settings, landings) and brings in the orch only when something goes wrong.
The same shape as loom today: the Go shed engine steps the run on its own (`lyx shed step --until-stop`), and the LLM driver above it wakes only when shed stops on something it cannot pass.
Per-task run settings (`config-layers-run-settings`) carry a task's review budgets and step models, so a start needs no LLM to set them.

## Two tiers, as in `go-driver-assistant` (2026-10-12)

`go-driver-assistant` (running) builds this shape for one loom run: a Go driver that settles stops by rule, a cold cheap assistant (the tackler) spawned only at a stop no rule settles, and the arbiter behind it.
The same two tiers fit the repo level:

1. A Go run driver: starts ready tasks with their `run_settings`, runs the landing routine (Land row, prod, intake), and posts what it cannot settle.
2. A spawnable assistant, cold per stop, never kept warm: it reads the stop and answers with a verdict or hands the question to the conversational orch.
   Scope and design choices always go to the orch.

Evidence from the loom level, a driver count over 98 runs (2026-10-05..12, 392 stops):

- plain relaunch 12 %; mechanical fix a Go rule could do 52 %; repair that needed an LLM 0 %;
- arbiter called 5 % (11 real attempts, all `resume`); relayed to the orch 22 %; other 10 %;
- drivers lived 370 h, 93 % of it idle.

The agent that ran the count estimated a cold helper would be needed at about 1 stop in 12 runs once Go takes the mechanical stops.
Nobody has counted the hub level yet: the orch's parent reviews, escalations, PR-Gates and landings by hand would need the same split before the Go share is known.

## A landing check for the Go run driver (operator, 2026-10-13)

At landing, loom warns that a task branch changed per-worktree config files (`_lyx/config/*.yaml`), which landing does not carry to the parent, and asks the parent to re-apply each change meant for it.
`logging-cleanup` raised it for a new, empty `_lyx/config/loom.yaml`: nothing to re-apply, and the orch found that only by diffing the file by hand.
The operator sees that check as a job for the Go run driver:

- parse the file at the fork base, the task tip and the parent tip, and compare keys;
- stay silent when the tip changes no key (an empty file, comments only) or the parent already holds the tip's value;
- otherwise name each changed key with its base, tip and parent values, so the parent knows exactly what to re-apply.

## Was `go-driven-shed`

## Question (operator, 2026-10-12)

How to get a Go-driven shed with an LLM watcher that steps in only when it must.

## Seen (2026-10-12)

The levels run their loops differently:

- batten: one task from Worktree-Create to Worktree-Teardown is a shed run that a Go process (`lyx batten run`) steps on its own, with no LLM; its `Run-Shed` row (engine `InnerRun`) starts the task's loom run and waits on it, and the orch gets a notice only when something stops.
- loom: the task's own shed run is stepped by `lyx shed step --until-stop`, but an LLM driver starts that command at once and waits in the background for the run to stop; the driver lives for the whole run.
- hub: the orch starts ready tasks, takes parent reviews, escalations and PR-Gates, and lands by hand where batten does not.

The operator wants the LLM involvement the same at every level.
At the hub level one LLM cannot keep a loop running for every batten run: too much for the orch to track (operator, 2026-10-12), so the hub loop must be Go, as `orch-split` proposes.

## Idea

One pattern at every level: a Go loop always runs, and an LLM watcher is spawned cold only when the loop stops on something it cannot pass.

- loom: `Run-Shed` steps the task's shed run in Go itself, instead of starting a driver that starts the loop.
  On an unexpected stop it spawns the watcher with the stop report, the way `driver-arbiter` already spawns a cold agent for a stop the driver cannot settle.
- hub: a Go loop starts ready tasks with their run settings and lands finished ones; the hub watcher wakes only on what it cannot settle (`orch-split`).
- Planned stops (parent review, PR-Gate) become cold agents Go spawns, which `alignment-agent` builds.

## Gains

- No long-lived driver session per run, which today can stall after a host sleep, run out of context or keep an old binary after a deploy (`board-field-drop`).
- Few tokens are saved: a waiting driver takes no turns.

## Open

- Who receives a message for a run when no driver lives for the whole run (`run-message-routing`): a queue the next agent reads, with lasting content going to the decision record.
- What the watcher may do: the driver's repair powers today, or fewer.
- Whether the watcher for a run is the same role at loom and hub level, with different scope.

## Was `run-message-routing`

Its open question is also in `go-driven-shed`'s Open above; delivery of the message stays with `creel` (triage, 2026-10-12).

Who in a running task receives an instruction from the orch or the operator, open for a brainstorm (operator, 2026-10-07).

Seen 2026-10-07: an operator decision about card 1 of `bugfix-sessions` arrived while Webster ran.
The orch has to know which agent owns the content at that moment (Discussion-Write, the plan agent, the Webster master, a Burler round) and message it, or fall back on a goto; mid-Webster no agent can change a begun card at all (`webster-amend-begun-card`).
The orch editing the run's files itself is never the answer.

Options raised:

- The driver forwards: it knows its current producer and the strand doing the work. One address per run, but an LLM relays in a turn of its own, may reword, and its stencil does not do this today.
- An alias such as `ly:<slug>:active` for the strand that owns the current step: deterministic, no LLM between.
  Creel must not know what runs or what is active (operator): it owns messages and injects only.
  So creel could at most store a plain name-to-name alias that loom itself sets at every producer transition, knowing nothing of its meaning; or the alias lives outside creel altogether.
- An on-call LLM per run, woken when an instruction needs judgment about the run (what a decision means for the plan, who must do what). The operator considered this before the driver existed, when the driver was a Go process; it rebuilds its context each time it wakes, and it adds a role.
- The driver itself becomes that on-call role, with read access to the plan: it already lives the whole run, but grows heavier than a step driver.

Plain routing ("deliver to whoever works now") and judgment ("what does this mean for the run") may want different answers.

Steps with no LLM at all: the Go producers (Preflight, Batchifier, the verify gates, Publish, Finalize, teardown) have no strand to deliver to.
A message could wait in its queue for the next LLM producer if the alias is resolved at delivery rather than at send, but that agent may not be the right one (after Batchifier comes the Webster master, while the instruction may concern the plan).
This suggests a split to discuss:
- Content ("the settle comes from config") goes into the decision record, which is durable, read by every later LLM producer, and needs no live receiver.
- Only an instruction that must act now needs a live receiver, and the most urgent one, stop, is a run pause (`lyx batten pause`), which works during a Go step too.

Operator leaning (2026-10-07): the driver takes the message.
Operator 2026-10-12: agrees that the driver takes it.
It runs a Sonnet agent on purpose, to have judgment; it is the one LLM alive for the whole run, Go steps included, it knows where the run stands, and it receives messages while its `shed step` runs in the background.
With a message it could record content with `lyx loom decision add` (a lyx verb, not a source edit), forward it to the strand that owns the current step, or pause the run or ask for a goto.

Refined (operator, 2026-10-07): every instruction for a run is posted to its driver, which gets only the short reminder (sender and subject) and does not read the body by default.
Knowing which agent works now, it either reads it itself or forwards it with `lyx creel forward` (see the `creel` note), so the receiving agent talks to the original sender, not to the driver: a minimal routing job.

entries.title: lyx orch start --continue resumes the last orch session
entries.brief: lyx orch records its session id so a reboot resumes the same orch conversation instead of a fresh one.
entries.body:
Split out of note `orch-owns-the-loop` (2026-10-11).

After a reboot the operator wants the same conversation back, as `claude --continue` gives, not a fresh session reading a handoff.
Today that takes `lyx orch start --adopt <session-id>`, with the id dug out of `~/.claude/projects/`.
`lyx orch` records its session id and offers `lyx orch start --continue` (or makes it the default for a dead strand) to adopt the last orch session.

entries.title: Scoped build and test for C# hubs on Windows
entries.brief: Verify gates in a .NET hub build and test only the projects a card touches, since a scanned Windows machine makes every build slow.
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-12)

The operator will use LoomYard for C# development on a Windows work machine.
There Millhouse's mill-go often takes about 2 hours for implementation alone, against a median of 27 minutes on this Go codebase.
The machine runs Cortex XDR, which scans every file write and process start, and IT allows no scan exclusions, so every build and test run is slow.
On that machine, narrowly scoped testing is what decides how long a run takes.

## Want

The verify gates in a .NET hub build and test only what a card or batch touches, as `lyx gate test` scopes Go packages here:

- map changed code to the tests that exercise it, and run only those with `dotnet test --filter`.
  Unlike Go, where a package's tests sit in the package, C# tests live in separate test projects, often one large project for many production projects, so picking test projects alone narrows little (operator, 2026-10-12).
  Candidate maps: test classes that reference the changed symbols (from the index, quarry), naming conventions (`FooTests` for `Foo`), or coverage-based test impact analysis;
- restore once per run, then build and test with `--no-restore` and incrementally;
- keep build processes warm (MSBuild node reuse, build server) so fewer processes start;
- run the whole solution once, at the final gate only.

## Open

- How a hub declares its language toolchain and the commands the gates run, and how much of today's Go-specific gate code this touches.
- Which map picks the tests, and how a missed test is caught: the final full-solution gate, or a card naming its tests under `Uses:`.
- A filtered run still builds the whole test project, so a large shared test project keeps a fixed build cost per gate.
- Measure on the work machine before and after: build and test minutes per run.

entries.title: lyx report timing: phase minutes, parent waits and agent spawns from run records
entries.brief: A mechanical per-run and per-day time report beside lyx report convergence, including stops by who settled them.
entries.body:
A mechanical time report over the hub's run records, beside `lyx report convergence`: today it took an LLM agent five minutes and an awk script to compute (2026-10-12).
The operator wants it as a tool, not an LLM job.

## What it reports

- Per run: minutes per phase (setup, Discussion, Plan, Webster, Merge, Publish to Finalize), total active minutes, minutes waiting on the parent or orch, and the span.
- Medians per phase over the landed runs in a window.
- Day or week totals: active run-minutes, parent waits (parent review, PR-Gate awaiting), arbiter spawns and minutes, alignment-agent spawns and minutes.
- Stops by who settled them: judge, shed, driver, arbiter, alignment agent, orch, operator.
  Fewer orch wakes alone can hide that load moved to the arbiter; the stop count itself shows whether runs converge.
  Check whether `lyx report convergence` already counts arbiter and alignment outcomes, and share its record reading.

## How the 2026-10-12 agent computed it

- Landed runs from the `archive/<slug>/*` tags in the records repository, runs in flight from `<slug>-weft`; each run's start from the hub `Seed-Child` row.
- History `at` stamps are completion times, so a row's interval runs from the previous row.
- Parent review windows from the round's `request.json` and `verdict.json`.
- Rework passes count in the phase of the producer that re-ran.
- Hibernation: a gap with no row from any run and no producer working; the journal's resume time confirms it.

## Data gaps found

- `attempt.json` `spawned_at` for alignment attempts is unreliable (later than the attempt's own report in `intake-bugs-1012`); archived attempts have no file mtimes.
- No token totals: `tools/tokencount` only runs through `go run`; review rounds' `round-N-usage.yaml` covers review agents only.
- Batten's Land delay after Friction-Reflect sits outside the run's own history (20.7 min for `plan-gate-fixes`).

entries.title: Audit glyph use in Webster, the kick-start pack first
entries.brief: Check from transcripts of a smaller task whether Webster forks use the kick-start pack and glyphs as intended
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-10-12)

Glyph use is probably not fully in place yet.
Analyse transcripts of a smaller task to see whether Webster uses glyphs as intended, above all the kick-start pack.

Plan's glyphs can be taken as sound for now (operator, 2026-10-12): the plan writer runs `lyx loom validate-plan` itself before it ends (step 5 of the plan stencil), the twill lens `forced-edits` checks each listed glyph against `lyx quarry`, and with twill a failed self-check cost one turn in three of six runs.

## First step: an A/B bench on the kick-start pack (operator, 2026-10-12)

Take a smaller task that has already landed and replay its Webster step in two separate worktrees, both checked out at the state right before Webster started (the parent commit plus the task's approved plan).
One arm runs with `kickstart_pack` on in `webster.yaml`, the other with it off; everything else, models included, is the same.
Compare per fork: turns, cache read, total weight, wall time, and whether the batch gates pass.
LLM runs vary, so run each arm more than once before reading a difference into it; the `twill-plan` bench (`docs/research/twill-plan-bench.md`) is the precedent for the setup.
The result decides whether the pack pays, and gives the baseline the two-prompt variant below is measured against.

## Was kickstart-pack-measure

This section describes the same with/without measurement of the kick-start pack as the bench above.

Seen at the PR-Gate review of plan-glyph-tuning (PR #559, 2026-10-11): the task built the Webster kick-start pack behind `webster.yaml` `kickstart_pack` (default on) and made it countable, but did not measure it.
Each begin-batch traces one `webster: kickstart pack` line (on, off or language-none, with resolved and unresolved counts), and each `plan:` handle traces one `webster: handle bind` line.

Idea: repeat the audit count on real loom runs with the pack on and off: grep-for-member calls and whole-file reads per implementer fork.
The Burler side of `kick-start-pack` and `enclose-kickstart` wait on this result.

This is an audit, not a loom run: an orch agent reads the Webster fork transcripts once a few loom runs have run with the pack on (it is on by default since `c279a38ba`), and compares them with the runs before it as the pack-off baseline.

### Result (audit, 2026-10-12)

Pack on: 35 implementer forks over 11 runs (150 cards); pack off: 113 forks over 43 runs (508 cards), 2026-10-08 to 2026-10-11; all on Sonnet.
Raw table and scripts: `.scratch/kickstart-measure/` in the hub prime.

- No measurable gain: calls before the first edit (median 6 on, 7 off), exploration calls per card (5.8 on, 5.9 off), turns and tokens are all within noise.
- The one consistent signal is about 20% fewer whole-file reads and greps, offset by more partial reads: pack spans replace whole-file reads rather than cutting exploration.
- Forks never used quarry lookups either way.
- Main confounder: forks inherit the Master's orientation, so a fork explores only about 6 calls before its first edit; most exploration is in the Master, which the pack does not reach.
  Pack quality also varies widely (1 to 144 resolved entries, up to 41 unresolved).

Verdict: the evidence does not justify building the Burler side yet.
The cheap next step, if wanted, is a controlled test: `kickstart_pack: false` for a few comparable runs.

### Next audit

`webster-pack-read-set` (landed `113593990`) reshaped the pack per card, but its fork still reads card by card, so it is not the version to measure.
Run the next audit once task `kickstart-read-all-first` has landed and a few loom runs have gone through Webster on it, compared against the runs before `113593990`.
Under read-all-first, calls before the first edit rise by construction, so compare exploration calls per card and total reads instead.

### Result (audit after read-all-first, 2026-10-13)

Read-all-first (`793c6a8ee`): 29 forks over 13 runs (125 cards), against 114 pack-off forks and 41 old-pack forks; all Sonnet.
Report, data and scripts: `.scratch/glyph-audit-2/` in the hub prime.

- Exploration calls per card are unchanged (5.8, against 5.8 old pack and 5.2 no pack): a solid result.
- Reads per card fell about 20 % (whole-file reads 3.5 to 2.0), turns per card 17–18 to 14.7, cache read 15–25 % lower; suggestive only, on mixed task sizes.
- 15 of 29 forks read in parallel in their first work turn (7 of 41 before); 9 still read serially.
- Quarry: 0 lookups with a pack; 19 of 114 pack-off forks used it.
- Unresolved pack entries are 35 % of the median pack, almost all `plan:` handles for members a card creates.

Verdict: do not build the Burler side yet.
Cheap next step: the end-of-prompt variant (the one-turn instruction and the pack as the prompt's last section), measured with the same scripts by the share of forks reading in parallel in the first work turn and exploration calls per card; the two-prompt variant only if the serial share stays high.

### Was `kick-start-pack`

The Burler side waits on the Webster pack measurement above (triage, 2026-10-12).

Read the closed GitHub issues #227 (implementer prompt) and #228 (Burler, with the operator's architecture-correction comment: inject once before the explore phase so every fork inherits it). Measured basis in quarry's `results/2026-09-06-kickstart` (`bench/loomyard-eval/ladder/results/2026-09-06-kickstart/conclusion.md`, commit `d2e492d`).

### Scope left here: Burler

The Webster implementer pack moved into task `plan-glyph-tuning` (2026-10-11), which also makes the pack switchable by config.
What stays here is the Burler side from #228: a pack of the reviewed glyphs injected once before the reviewer's explore phase, so every lens fork inherits it.
Take it up once the Webster pack has run with and without the pack and shown whether it helps.

### The pack is the read set (was note pack-is-the-read-set)

Seen in fan-lab 2026-10-10: a solo `opus[medium]` reviewer given a kick-start pack ("read all listed spans first") read the pack and then explored about 20 more tool calls, so the pack came on top of exploration instead of replacing it.
Neither the prompt nor the ladder card said to stay with the pack.

The reviewer prompt says the pack is the read set:
- the reviewer reads the pack's spans and treats them as read;
- any read beyond them needs a named gap (a caller or spawned process one hop out), within a small tool-call budget;
- the reviewer ends with one line per extra read saying why the pack lacked it (the fork rule from `fan-master-preread` variant D).

## What to check in Webster

- The kick-start pack (`internal/websterengine/doc.go`, "the kick-start pack"): how many refs resolved and how many did not (the `webster: kickstart pack` Info line per begin-batch), and why the unresolved ones failed.
- Whether the implementer fork reads the listed spans in its first turn as FRESH-READ says, or re-reads whole files, greps or runs `lyx quarry` for members the pack already resolved.
- Whether a fork edits outside the listed spans, and whether that work rests on stale reads.
- The `deviations` a fork reports against what `ScopeGuard` finds (`webster-deviations-list`).

## The fork prompt (operator, 2026-10-12)

A Webster fork prompt (`reed-multi-window`, batch 01) runs to about 311 lines; the kick-start pack starts near line 114.
The one-turn instruction stands only in the FRESH-READ rule, far above the pack; the pack's own heading explains its entry format instead, and step 1 restates FRESH-READ.
The operator doubts the pack has any effect as it is delivered today.

Idea to test once the audit shows how forks read: two prompts instead of one.
The first carries the background (role, rules, cards, gates, report); the second says only "read all of this in one turn, in parallel, before any edit" followed by the pack.
That costs a turn, but the read is then the only thing the fork is told to do in that turn.
The first prompt can end with "now read `<file>` and do what it says", so no second message is needed: the second prompt is a file (operator, 2026-10-12).
A cheaper variant to compare: one prompt whose last section is the one-turn instruction and the pack, since the end of a prompt is what an agent acts on first.

## Seen

`webster-deviations-list`: a Webster fork's `deviations` list mixed in files that probably house its batch's own target glyphs, because the implementer stencil asks it to compare against the glyph union and also tells it not to.

entries.title: Make shuttle and lyx neutral to the LLM provider
entries.brief: Engine registry, engine in run.json, no Claude names in the core, usage readers behind the engine
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-10-13)

Everything about driving an LLM is meant to go through shuttle, so a new provider (Codex CLI first, `codex-engine`) should need only one more engine.
Rewrite shuttle and the other modules so that holds: lyx is neutral to the LLM, not tailored to Claude Code.

## Seen (feasibility study, 2026-10-13)

Report `docs/research/codex-feasibility.md`. Couplings outside the engine interface:

- The engine choice is hardwired at about 15 call sites (the `wiring.go` files of burlercli, webstercli and loomcli, `loomcli/looparm.go`, `orchcli/cli.go`, `battencli/wire.go`, `pausecli/deps.go`, `shuttlecli/cli.go`, `cliwire/sessionnamer.go`, `shuttleengine/rundir.go`).
  `modelspec` has an `Engine` field, but only `claude` is accepted and nothing reads the resolved engine.
- `run.json` records no engine, so readers over many runs assume one.
- `shuttleengine/hold.go`'s hold-notice text names `SendMessage`: a provider leak into the core.
- tokencount and the timing report read `~/.claude/projects` and carry Claude prices.
- Deploy syncs skills only into `~/.claude/plugins`.
- Stencils assume Claude Code features: Agent-tool forks, `SendMessage`/`ListAgents`, background Bash that wakes the session.
- Smaller: `CleanClaudeEnv` in reed, `claude_*` config keys, session naming, CLAUDE.md counted in Merriam's base.

## Scope to discuss

- An engine registry chosen per role through model specs, the engine recorded in `run.json`, multi-run readers that pick the reader per run.
- Provider-neutral wording in core notices; provider-specific text only in the engine.
- Usage and transcript readers behind the engine, so tokencount and timing work for any engine.
- Which stencil features get a neutral form (a parent directive that does not rely on `SendMessage`) and which stay Claude-only, refused for other engines.

entries.title: Tune the Burler lens fan prompts
entries.brief: Revisit the parked lens fan with lens and fork prompts that overlap less, measured against solo on the fan-lab fixtures
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-10-13)

The Burler lens fan is parked because the fan-lab bench found it no better than a solo round, and its forks found mostly overlapping findings.
The operator thinks the fan could pay with better-tuned prompts: lenses and fork instructions that send each fork after different defects.

## Starting point

- The operator's first bench of Burler's fan, when it was designed, found a fair amount, though mostly less advanced defects; twill, built after it, proved clearly more effective (operator, 2026-10-13).
  Twill's forks share the writer's context and their findings are judged by the writer, which may be the design to borrow.
- Bench results: `docs/research/lens-fan-lab-phase1.md` ("Conclusion") and `lens-fan-lab-phase0.md`, cost in `lens-fan-cost-analysis.md`.
- On Discussion-Review a `sonnet[medium]` fan missed the BLOCKING defect that solo `opus[medium]` found; a `sonnet[high]` fan found it but passed 300k context and cost more than solo.
- On Plan-Review the `sonnet[high]` fan's surplus was mostly LOW findings, at about six times a solo round's cost.
- Variant D's master manifest (pre-read without judging) is the report's named starting point if the fan is revisited.
- Forks inherit the reviewer session's model (`fan_review`), so master and forks cannot run on different models.

## Scope to discuss

- Lens texts that overlap less: what each lens owns, and what it must leave to the others.
- Measure overlap per lens against the solo round's findings, on the fan-lab fixtures, before any hub setting changes.
- Fan on or off per round (for instance fan in round 1 only) needs code; see `model-downgrade` for per-round models.

entries.title: Lighter test rules for small changes
entries.brief: Tests that pin stencil wording make small prompt changes large; pin only what must hold, measured first
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-10-13)

The project's test and doc rules make small changes large.
`webster-pack-last` moved the kick-start pack into a file of its own: about 70 lines of change, about 140 lines of tests and about 20 lines of required docs and registration, 14 files in all.

## Seen

- Tests that pin stencil wording (`contracts/stencils/claims_test.go`, the template tests such as `internal/websterengine/template_test.go`) change with every sentence a prompt changes, and prompt changes are much of today's work.
- The doc rule (`doc.go` in the same commit) is cheap and keeps the package docs true.

## Options to discuss

1. Tests pin only what must hold: markers, file paths, order and the presence of load-bearing rules, not the wording of sentences.
2. Stencil wording claims move from tests to review: the Burler review checks them instead.
3. Keep the doc rule, but drop the per-card test requirement for stencil-only changes.

## First step

Count, over the landed tasks of the last weeks, how much of each diff is tests that pin stencil or template wording, against the code change itself, so the choice rests on numbers.

entries.title: Verification protocol for a .NET repo: slow-suite tier, numerical-baseline capture/compare, verify timeouts and logs
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #609](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/609).

## Summary

NORCE-DrillingAndWells/Models (C#/.NET 9, NUnit) is about to move from Millhouse to LoomYard.
LoomYard's plan-level `## verify:` gate covers this repo's ordinary test suite.
It does not cover the rest of the repo's verification protocol: a gated slow suite, and a **numerical-baseline capture/compare harness** whose reference must be captured *before* the first code change and compared at the end.
This issue describes, as concretely as possible, what the repo needs from the tool, what it does today by hand or through Millhouse, and the failure modes seen in practice.
Items are marked **required** (the repo cannot be developed safely without it) or **wanted**.

## Repo facts the tool has to know

- **Project root is not the git root.** Everything runs from `src/csharp/NORCE.Models/` (it holds `NORCE.Models.sln`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.scratch/`, the task-state dir). Verify commands, scratch paths and baseline paths are relative to that directory, never to the git root.
- **Several task worktrees run at the same time**, under `<container>/wts/<slug>/`, often three to five at once, each building and testing. They share one machine.
- **Plain `dotnet test` on the solution is safe:** the two gated projects set `IsTestProject=false` unless their MSBuild property is passed, so the solution run only runs the fast suite.
- Test namespaces are flat (`NORCE.Models.Tests`), so `--filter FullyQualifiedName~X` matches a **class** name, not a folder.

## The three test projects

| Project | Gate | Runtime (quiet machine, 2026-10-14) | When it must run |
|---|---|---:|---|
| `NORCE.Models.Tests` | none | ~2 min, 1537 tests | every implementation attempt (the plan-level verify) |
| `NORCE.Models.SlowTests` | `-p:RunSlowTests=true` | ~2 min, 21 tests | once at finalization, before the PR |
| `NORCE.Models.NumericalBaseline` | `-p:RunBaseline=true` | ~9 s, 8 fixtures | twice: capture before the first change, verify at finalization |

A full solution build is ~30 s.
Under three parallel worktrees the fast suite was observed at 2.5–3.7 min per run.
The full per-test table is in `src/csharp/NORCE.Models/doc/test-suite-runtime.md` in that repo.

## Required 1: a second must-pass gate tier for the slow suite

The plan-level verify is the fast suite. The slow suite must also pass before the PR, but running it on every gate attempt doubles the attempt cost for no gain.

Needed:
- A verify tier that runs **once, at landing** (before Describe/Publish), not per attempt: `dotnet test NORCE.Models.SlowTests -p:RunSlowTests=true --nologo -clp:ErrorsOnly`.
- Same rerun-once flakiness policy and the same timeout behaviour as the existing gate; failures go back to a fixer the same way.
- Configured per repo (the command lives in repo config, not in each plan), since it never varies between tasks.
- **Zero discovered tests is a failure.** Running a gated project without its property discovers nothing and still exits green. A gate that reads the exit code alone passes vacuously if the flag is dropped. The gate must check that the run discovered tests (e.g. a minimum count, or parse the `Total:` line / the TRX).

## Required 2: numerical-baseline capture/compare as a first-class step

This is the part with no LoomYard equivalent today, and the one most likely to be gotten wrong by an agent.

### What the harness is

`NORCE.Models.NumericalBaseline` runs five purpose-built regression programs plus fixtures and string-compares their scrubbed console output against stored files. It is **not a test suite**: one run proves nothing.

- **Capture:** `dotnet test NORCE.Models.NumericalBaseline -p:RunBaseline=true --nologo`. With no baseline present, every fixture reports `Inconclusive` and writes `<Fixture>.<Method>.txt` plus `_source.txt` (commit, branch, dirty flag, timestamp) into `.scratch/numerical-baseline/` beside `CLAUDE.md`. `.scratch/` is gitignored; baselines are deliberately never committed.
- **Verify:** same command plus `-e NORCE_BASELINE_MODE=verify`. A missing baseline is a hard failure, never an invitation to record one. A deviation fails with the first differing index, the baseline path and the source commit.
- **Side capture for diagnosis:** `-e NORCE_BASELINE_DIR=<absolute dir>` writes the post-change output into a separate directory, so the two directories can be diffed fixture by fixture without touching the trusted one.

### What the tool must do

1. **Capture at the branch point, in the task worktree, before the first code change.** The worktree HEAD at spawn *is* the reference. Capture runs right after the worktree is created (or as the first step of implementation), on the code already checked out.
   - Never check out a second copy to capture from: no `git worktree add`, no clone, nothing under `.scratch/` or the task-state dir. (Millhouse did exactly this once, Millhouse #1181: a nested checkout under `.scratch/verify-baseline-<hash>/`, 8x slower and a corruption risk for the outer repo. It is fixed there; LoomYard must not repeat it.)
   - If code has already changed when the step runs, **do not capture**. Say so and halt: a baseline taken from half-implemented code can only bless drift, never detect it.
2. **Trust check before reusing an existing baseline.** Read `_source.txt`; the recorded commit must be the branch point. The `dirty:` flag is coarse (any untracked file sets it, including the tool's own task-state files), so judge by `git diff <commit> -- '*.cs'` being empty, not by the flag.
3. **Verify at landing**, after the slow tier, with `NORCE_BASELINE_MODE=verify`. A capture-mode run reports every fixture `Inconclusive`; the gate must not read that as a pass. Verify mode reports `Passed`.
4. **On deviation, halt for the operator; never auto-fix and never auto-refresh.**
   - Capture the post-change output into `.scratch/numerical-baseline-post/` with `NORCE_BASELINE_DIR`, diff the two directories, and surface the diff fixture by fixture in plain terms.
   - The operator decides whether the drift is intended. **Intended drift is common:** most physics fixes in this repo move numbers on purpose, and the PR then explains the drift per fixture.
   - The tool must **never delete or overwrite a baseline file to make a comparison pass.** A refresh is an explicit operator command, and it backs up the old directory (e.g. `.scratch/numerical-baseline-pre-refresh/`) before recapturing.
5. **Carry the outcome into the change description**: "no drift" or the per-fixture drift summary, as a check item for the PR reviewer, alongside the verify-gate triage sections.
6. **Optional per-batch drift snapshots** (wanted, not required): capturing into `.scratch/numerical-baseline-after-batch-N/` after each batch made it possible to say which batch moved which fixture. Cheap (~9 s) and diagnostic only; never a gate.

### Why this matters

The fast and slow suites assert physics properties; they do not detect a silent numerical shift. The baseline is the only instrument that does. A gate that runs it once, or captures at the wrong moment, is vacuous and looks green.

## Required 3: verify timeouts and observable verify runs

Observed under Millhouse on 2026-10-13: the background baseline pre-flight (which ran the fast suite once, ~2 min when run directly) took **87 min** in one task, 22 min (three commands) in another, 7 min in a third. The cause is unknown, because the log lived inside the worktree and was gone after teardown, and the run had no timeout (`baseline_verify_timeout_minutes: null`). Direct reproduction attempts (pipe capture of `dotnet test` and of a full rebuild) closed normally.

Needed (LoomYard already fails a timed-out gate without rerun; these are the surrounding pieces):
- **A default timeout** on every verify run, set per tier in repo config (fast ~10 min, slow ~10 min, baseline ~3 min here), never "no ceiling" by default.
- **Per-run timing in the log:** command, cwd, start, end, wall seconds, exit code, discovered/passed/failed counts.
- **Logs that survive teardown**, in the reports directory or the archive, so a slow run can be diagnosed after landing.
- Wall time of each verify run listed in the run's final summary, so a regression in suite runtime is visible without digging.

## Wanted 4: fewer full-suite runs per task

One task (eight fixes, several batches) ran the full fast suite about 15 times, ~35 min, through implementer, fixer and review rounds. LoomYard's single plan-level verify per attempt already helps. Beyond that:
- Let an implementer's in-batch check be **scoped** (`--filter FullyQualifiedName~<Class>`) and keep the full suite to the gate.
- **Skip the gate for a verified tree:** LoomYard's verified-tree record already does this; it should also cover the slow tier and the baseline verify, keyed on the tree hash, so a Describe/landing step after a passing gate reruns nothing.
- **Doc-only diffs skip all test tiers**: when the diff touches only `*.md` (no `*.cs`, `*.csproj`, `*.sln`), no suite runs.

## Wanted 5: exclusivity for timing work, and only for it

Timing measurements (BenchmarkDotNet runs, before/after tables recorded as deliverables) are invalid if any other worktree is building or testing. Correctness runs are fine in parallel, only slower.
- A container-wide **exclusive lock** a task can take for a timing run, which other tasks' verify runs wait on (and only those, not their agents).
- Never serialize correctness runs.

## Wanted 6: one build, several tiers

The tiers can share one build: `dotnet build NORCE.Models.sln -p:RunSlowTests=true -p:RunBaseline=true`, then each tier with `--no-build`. This saves ~30 s per extra tier at landing. If the tool builds once, the gate properties must be passed to the build too, or the gated projects build as non-test projects and discover nothing (see Required 1, zero-tests-is-failure).

## Repo rules a reviewer rubric should be able to check

Not tool features, but things a configurable review checklist should carry for this repo:
- No test in any of the three projects runs, mirrors or references a `Program*` demonstration (`NORCE.Models.Program`). Check with a grep of the test projects for `Program0NN_`.
- Comparisons against stored output live in `NORCE.Models.NumericalBaseline` alone; an in-process test may byte-compare two arms it builds itself.
- No argument guards (`ThrowIfNull`, range checks) and no try/catch around the repo's own code.

## Acceptance

A LoomYard task in this repo, run end to end, without the agent being told any of the above:
1. captures the numerical baseline in its own worktree before the first code change, with `_source.txt` naming the branch point;
2. runs the fast suite as the plan-level gate, with a timeout and logged timing;
3. at landing, runs the slow suite once and the baseline in verify mode, refusing zero-test and Inconclusive outcomes;
4. on baseline drift, halts with a per-fixture diff and waits for the operator, never touching the baseline;
5. puts the drift outcome and each tier's wall time in the change description;
6. leaves its verify logs where they survive teardown.


## Issue comment, 2026-10-14

## Addendum: run the pre-implementation captures detached

Everything that must run on the branch point can start **detached at spawn** and run while discussion and planning go on. No code changes until implementation starts, so the tree is the right reference for the whole window. Two runs qualify:

- the numerical-baseline capture (`dotnet test NORCE.Models.NumericalBaseline -p:RunBaseline=true --nologo`, ~10 s plus build);
- any pre-existing-failure reference for the verify gate (the fast suite once, ~2 min), if LoomYard keeps one. It can also skip this when the parent tip is already a verified tree.

Requirements on the detached job:

1. **It starts at spawn, on the spawn HEAD**, and records that commit. Discussion and plan write only task-state files, which do not affect the run. The `_source.txt` dirty flag will be set by those files, so the trust check compares `*.cs` against the recorded commit, not the flag.
2. **Implementation waits for it before the first code edit.** A batch must not start while the capture is running: an edit mid-capture gives a reference that is part old code and part new. Normally the job finished long before, so the wait costs nothing.
3. **A failed or timed-out capture halts before implementation.** It never falls back to capturing later, because a capture after the first edit can only bless drift.
4. **It has the timeout and per-run log from Required 3**, and the log survives teardown. The 87-minute case was exactly this kind of detached pre-flight job, with no ceiling and a log that disappeared with the worktree.
5. **It builds with the gate properties** (`-p:RunBaseline=true`, plus `-p:RunSlowTests=true` if the slow tier shares the build), and it does not hold a lock that blocks the agent's own work while it runs.

With that, verification adds nothing to the critical path before implementation. The only verification time left on the critical path is the gate after each attempt and the landing tiers.

entries.title: Run verbs in one shared namespace, not under lyx loom
entries.brief: lyx loom decision/status/goto/approve act on darn runs too; move recipe-neutral run verbs to one shared namespace
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-14)

Since `0850f76e` a darn run has a decision record, and `lyx loom decision add` works on it.
The operator finds it absurd that a `loom` command acts on something that is not a loom run.
The same holds for the other run verbs the orch uses on darn runs: `lyx loom status`, `goto`, `resume`, `approve`, `reject`, `start`, `review approve`.

## Direction (operator, 2026-10-14)

Darn and loom are both shed recipes and are to be handled the same way.
Verbs that act on any run move to one shared namespace, and `lyx loom` keeps only what is loom's own.
Not `lyx shed`: shed is only the FSM and knows nothing about decisions, reviews or approvals (operator).
For now the verbs stay under `lyx loom` (operator, 2026-10-14).

## Open

- The shared namespace's name, and which module owns it: the layer above shed that both recipes share (decision record, parent review, approve and reject) has no module of its own today; `internal/loomcli` serves darn runs too.
- Which verbs are recipe-neutral and which are loom's own.
- Every stencil, way-forward text and doc that names `lyx loom <verb>` for a darn run changes with it.
- Relates to `perch-budget-arbiter`, which gives darn and loom one config shape for review budgets.

entries.title: Show the orch context size in the prime overview window
entries.brief: The prime overview window shows the orch session context tokens against its thresholds beside the batten runs
entries.body:
## Ask (operator, 2026-10-14)

The operator wants the orch's context size easy to see, in the prime's overview window beside the batten runs.

## Today

- The prime's overview window runs `lyx batten overview` (`internal/battencli/overview.go`), one line per batten run in flight.
- The orch's context size is read by the distill watcher (`internal/orchengine/watcher.go`, `ContextTokens` in `internal/shuttleengine/claudeengine/usage.go`) and stored as `LastContextTokens` in the orch state (`internal/orchengine/state.go`).
- It is shown only by `lyx orch status` (`context_tokens`, `soft_threshold_tokens`, `threshold_tokens`); no pane or statusline shows it.

## Sketch

- The batten overview gains a line for the orch: context tokens against the soft and hard thresholds, plus the watcher's phase and cycle count, read from the orch state file it already sits beside (files only, as the overview reads today).
- Dependency direction to check: batten's overview reading orch state may cross a layer; if so, the orch line comes from a provider the orch module registers, or the runs strand runs a composed view.

entries.title: Clearer loom model key names, one per step
entries.brief: Model keys like fix name the role they set, and every review segment gets its own reviewer and fixer key
entries.body:
## Ask (operator, 2026-10-14)

The loom config's model keys say little about what they set: `fix` reads like a flag, not "the model of the fixer in a review round".
The operator wants clearer names, and a model per step rather than one shared value for all.

## Today (`internal/loomengine/template.yaml`)

- `review` and `fix` set the reviewer and fixer model of every review segment; each takes one spec or a per-round list.
- `discussion_review`/`discussion_fix`, `plan_review`/`plan_fix` and `webster_review`/`webster_fix` override them per segment; an empty value falls back to the shared key.
- The Merge segment has no keys of its own, so it always uses the shared `review` and `fix`.
- More role models sit beside them with the same naming style: `judge` and `seed` with per-segment `*_judge`/`*_seed`, `fan_review`, `rework`, `friction`, `driver`, `arbiter`, `tackler`, `alignment`.
- "review" also appears in non-model keys (`review_max_bounces`, `review_timeout_min`, `skip_merge_review`), which adds to the confusion.

## Idea

- Name each key after the role it sets, e.g. `reviewer_model`/`fixer_model`, `plan_reviewer_model`, so a model key reads as a model key.
- Give every review segment, Merge included, its own reviewer and fixer key, so each step is set explicitly; whether a shared fallback stays is open.
- `lyx config reconcile`/Migrate rewrites old keys to the new names.
- The shape (flat role names or a nested `models:` block per segment) is an operator choice still open.

entries.title: Spawned code roles load the hub language skills
