entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-14)

The darn writer of `delete-order-own-edit` writes Go but loaded only `scribe:prose` and `scribe:code-quality`.
No spawned code-writing or code-reviewing role loads a language skill:

- darn writer: `darnSkills` in `internal/darnengine/spec.go`, `scribe:prose`, `scribe:code-quality`; no `scribe:testing` either.
- Webster master and recovery: `roleSkills` in `internal/websterengine/roles.go`, `scribe:prose`, `scribe:code-quality`, `scribe:testing`.
- Burler seats: `burlerSkills` in `internal/burlerengine/engine.go`, the same three.
- Merge conflict resolution: `conflictSkills` in `internal/mergeresolve/spec.go`, `scribe:prose`, `scribe:code-quality`.

`scribe:golang-comments`, `scribe:golang-testing` and `scribe:golang-build` exist, and `pattern/PATTERN-test-economy.md` cites `scribe:golang-testing` as holding the general rules, yet no role gets them.

## Idea

- The hub's config names its language skills (e.g. Go: `scribe:golang-comments`, `scribe:golang-testing`, `scribe:golang-build`; a C# hub its `csharp-*` ones), since lyx serves hubs in other languages and must not hard-code Go.
- Each code-writing or code-reviewing role appends the hub's language skills to its own list; which roles get which (comments for writers and reviewers, testing for test writers, build for whoever runs the build) is to be decided.
- The darn writer also gains `scribe:testing`, as Webster and Burler have.

entries.title: A hub pause leaves background forks and shells running, so hibernate never confirms
entries.brief: Pause interrupts turns but not background forks or shells; sessions read busy and hibernate confirmation fails
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-14)

`lyx hibernate request` with no trigger paused the hub at once, but its confirmation never passed: after the grace, `lyx tender status` still read `ly:overview-seats:webster` and `ly:overview-seats:driver` as `busy` with cause `background`, and the orch as `busy` with cause `turn` while it answered the operator.

- The pause interrupts a session's running turn, but work the session started in the background keeps going: Webster's implementer forks, and the driver's background wait loop.
- A session with background work reads busy, so confirmation withholds until its ten-minute bound and the request fails.
- The operator cancelled the request and hibernated by hand.

## Idea

- A hub pause also stops, or lets finish and then holds, each session's background work: forks, background shells, Monitors; or confirmation treats a session whose only background work is a known-safe wait (the driver's loop) as idle.
- What a paused fork should do (stop and be re-spawned on resume, or finish its batch and write its report) needs a design choice, since killing an implementer fork mid-batch leaves a half-done batch for Webster's recovery.
- The orch's own turn should not withhold confirmation when the orch itself requested the hibernate and ends its turn.

## Operator view (2026-10-15, not a decision)

- Claude Code can pause a fork: the fork is picked in the terminal's fork/agent picker and stopped there, and the master is then told the fork stopped. A hub pause would have to reach each fork that way.
- Forks are not interrupted as a rule: Webster forks can live long (one ran 45 minutes on 2026-10-14), and cutting one off mid-batch is out of the question as a default.
- But that 45-minute fork held 300k+ tokens of context: its batch was too long, and interrupting and restarting it with a fresh context might have been cheaper.
  This points at a separate idea: a context bound on a Webster fork that ends it and restarts the rest of the batch fresh, which also gives a pause a clean place to stop.

entries.title: Bench fork0 and the strict critical fixer on twill Discussion-Write
entries.brief: Arms: twill as is, with the strict critical fixer, and fork0 plus the critical fixer, graded against Discussion-Review keys
entries.body:
## Ask (operator, 2026-10-15)

Bench fork0 and the strict critical fixer on twill's Discussion-Write, as the Plan-Write benches did on 2026-10-14.
The operator designed twill mainly for Discussion, to give a far more solid first draft, and holds that a watertight Discussion saves the most later in a run.
On Plan-Write the gain came above all from tightening the prompt of the part that makes the changes the lens forks reported: the agent doing it must doubt every finding.

## Today

- Discussion-Write runs twill (`discussion_producer: twill`) with the `twill-discussion` lens fan in `internal/burlerengine/template.yaml`, unchanged since twill landed (`50cf6a425`) and benched once (`docs/research/twill-discussion-bench.md`).
- The task `twill-fork0` builds fork0 for Plan-Write only; its Discussion auto-picked fork0 out of Discussion-Write because no bench measured it there, and applies the critical judge to Discussion-Write without a bench.

## Bench

- Fresh agent, the same method as `docs/research/twill-fixer-bench.md` and `docs/research/twill-fork0-bench.md`: references with known Discussion-Review findings as the key, arms spliced into the Discussion-Write prompt by a wrapper, runs stopped after Discussion-Write, one grader in one pass.
- Arms:
  - a: twill as it is (writer writes, then lens forks, then the writer fixes).
  - c: a with the strict critical fixer (doubt every finding, two-sided weighing).
  - f: fork0 (the master explores and interviews, fork0 writes the draft, the master spawns the blind lens forks and fixes as the strict critical fixer).
- Measure: findings real/noise, wrong dispositions, key items repeated in the final discussion, cost and time per arm.
- Question for arm f: the master holds the interview context the fork does not, so whether fork0 loses anything at Discussion is the point to grade.

## Timing

Open: bench on a prototype wrapper now, as the Plan benches did, or after `twill-fork0` lands, so the bench runs on its built critical judge.

entries.title: Run status pane: numbered rows, seconds, round totals, gate time; segment-named sessions
entries.brief: Per-run status pane shows seconds, a total per Burler round, and each gate with its time and the rework it caused
entries.body:
## Seen

The per-run status pane (the checklist each run's window shows, rendered through `internal/statuspane` and `internal/loomcli/checklist.go`) gives each row's time in whole minutes (`statuspane.FormatMinutes`).
A Burler review round shows its parts (review seats, fix) each with its own time, but no total for the round.
Gate refusals, and the rework they cause, do not show at all.

## Wanted

Operator's requests (2026-10-15), each in scope:

1. Show seconds as well as minutes for each row's time.
2. Give each Burler round a total time for the round, beside the time of each part.
3. Show the gates in the pane, with the time each gate took, and how much time went to rework because a gate refused (the rerun of the producer the gate sent back).
4. Number the pane's entries, for every shed-driven run (loom, darn, batten and any later recipe), not only loom.
   A shed recipe has a fixed list of rows, so each row gets its number.
   A perch (a Bouncer row with its Burler rounds) is one row of the recipe and so takes one number; its bounces are rounds within that entry, not new numbers.
5. Give every spawned session a name that says which segment it serves.
   Today the Bouncer and Burler sessions of Discussion, Plan and Webster carry the same names (for example strand `ly:twill-fork0:bouncer-seed`), so they cannot be told apart.
   The segment goes into the name both in the pane and in the reed strand and window names the operator switches between with Alt+Up/Down.

Items 4 and 5 were added by the operator on 2026-10-15.

If item 3 cannot be read from the records a run keeps today, the writer says what is missing in the PR description and ships items 1 and 2 with as much of item 3 as the records allow.

entries.title: Fork the Burler fixer from the reviewer session
entries.brief: The fixer re-reads the context the reviewer just read; fork it from the reviewer to reuse the cache
entries.body:
## Seen

Carried over from the removed note `model-downgrade` (2026-10-15).
Each Burler fixer is a fresh session that reads the whole context the reviewer just read, part of the $1.9 per run in the Burler cost breakdown.
Skipping the fixer on an empty review is already built (`internal/burlerengine/fix.go`).

## Idea

Fork the fixer from the reviewer's session, so it inherits the reviewer's cache prefix instead of reading the context again.
A fork inherits the reviewer's model, so this rules out a separate fixer model for a forked fixer.

## Other open items from `model-downgrade`

- Plan and Discussion fixers to `sonnet[medium]`: estimated about $4 over six runs, not benched.
- Fan on or off per round (fan in round 1, solo after) does not exist and needs code.
- A per-batch Webster model (a cheap model only for mechanical cards) needs code in `internal/websterengine`.

entries.title: Webster fork read audit as a tool under tools/
entries.brief: Move the 2026-10-13 fork read audit jq scripts out of scratch into a repeatable tools/ script
entries.body:
## Seen

The Webster fork read audit of 2026-10-13 (board note `glyph-use-audit`) ran on jq scripts: `extract2.jq` pulls per-fork rows from Webster implementer fork transcripts (pack parsing, edits, first-turn reads), `stats-base.jq`, `stats2.jq` and `stats3.jq` aggregate them, and by-hand steps build `files.txt`, `table.tsv` and `turns.tsv`.
Since `290c773d0` the scripts, the report and a README with the re-run recipe sit in `docs/research/glyph-audit-2026-10-13/`.
The README names the steps that were never recorded: how `files.txt` was built, the exact `extract2.jq` invocation, the script that produced `turns.tsv`, and the commands behind the pack-quality figures.

Operator view (2026-10-15), not a decision: scripts like these must be kept in the repository, not in scratch.

## Idea

A repeatable tool under `tools/`, like `tools/tokencount/tokencount.sh`: one script that takes a date range or a list of runs, finds the Webster implementer fork transcripts, and reports per fork whether it read its pack's spans in one parallel first work turn, plus exploration calls per card, split by pack on or off and, once `webster-pack-layout-switch` lands, by pack layout from the begin-batch trace line.

entries.title: Run window stays on shell: follow the overview and newest agent from run start
entries.brief: A viewer attached before any overview or agent window exists rests on shell and never follows the run
entries.body:
## Seen

On 2026-10-15 the operator's run window for the darn run `seed-ide-interactive-chain` sat on the `shell` window for the whole run.
It never moved to the overview (`loom-status`) or to the driver and `darn` agent windows as they spawned.
The same complaint has come up before: window auto-switching during runs is still unreliable.

## Why, by the documented rules

The focus rules in `internal/reedengine/doc.go` say that no automatic switch moves a viewer off the shell.
Batten's Open-Window row attaches the Konsole window right after Seed-Child, before the run has spawned its overview or any agent.
Attach selects `relevantWindow`, which is none at that moment, so the viewer stays on `shell`.
After that, the overview window is never selected, and a new agent window is selected only from the overview, a dead agent window, the relevant window or a driver window.
A viewer that landed on the shell by default is treated like one the operator moved there by hand, so it never follows the run.
A second possible cause: VS Code's folderOpen task chain also runs `lyx reed attach` (issue #633, task `seed-ide-interactive-chain`), and attach appends no `select-window` when another client is already attached.

## Wanted (operator)

When a run starts, the operator's window goes to the overview.
As the run spawns agents, it moves to the newest agent.
The shell is never where the window rests when a run starts.

## Operator decision (2026-10-15): a follow toggle

A per-session follow state, shown as a clickable button on the reed status bar:

- Follow is on when a run starts: the viewer goes to the overview, then to each newest agent window, from the shell too.
- Any window change the operator makes by hand (a status-bar click, Alt+Up/Down) turns follow off, and the button shows it off.
  Reed owns those bindings, so it can tell a manual switch from its own.
  A viewer the operator moved deliberately, for example to the shell, is then never disturbed.
- Clicking the button turns follow back on and jumps to the newest agent window, else the overview.

The button is one entry in the configurable button set of note `reed-status-buttons`.

entries.title: Configurable action buttons on the reed status bar
entries.brief: Clickable status-bar buttons that run configured commands: VS Code, orch distill/refresh, the follow toggle and more
entries.body:
## Idea

tmux status lines support clickable ranges (`#[range=user|<name>]` with a `MouseDown1Status` binding), and reed already uses them for its window buttons.
The same mechanism can carry action buttons that run a command when clicked.

Examples the operator named on 2026-10-15:

- open the pair in VS Code (`lyx ide spawn <slug>`),
- `lyx orch distill` and `lyx orch refresh` for the orch session,
- the follow toggle of note `viewer-off-shell`,
- "and much else".

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-15)

The button set must be highly and easily configurable, not a fixed list in code.

## Open design points

- Where the set lives: presumably reed's module config, with a hub default and per-session overrides (the orch session needs other buttons than a task pair).
- What a button entry holds: a label, the command, and which sessions show it.
- How a command runs: `run-shell` in the pair's worktree, with its output and failure visible somewhere.
- Whether the follow toggle is a built-in entry in the same set.

## Placement: options discussed on 2026-10-15, none chosen

Reed's status bar today has two lines: line 0 holds the window buttons (overview, agents, shell), line 1 the session buttons and the time.
The action buttons must not mix with the window buttons.
The operator worries that a separate line next to the others invites misclicks, above all on actions that cannot be undone, such as `lyx orch distill` and `lyx orch refresh`.

1. One menu button (my recommendation, the orch's call, not the operator's): a single button with a distinct look opens a tmux `display-menu` holding the configured actions.
   A misclick only opens the menu.
   The follow toggle, which is harmless to click, can sit beside it as a button of its own.
2. A third status line of action buttons, with `confirm-before` on the destructive ones.
   It is quicker to use, but each misclick costs a dismissal.
3. The right side of line 1, before the time: no extra row, but cramped with many sessions and buttons.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-15)

Prototype the placement and the menu by hand in a separate throwaway tmux server, never in a live reed session, before this becomes a task.

entries.title: Begin-batch refusal route and label; bare lyx config writes an empty layer
entries.brief: Two small bugs: a delete-before-reference refusal is mislabelled plan_drifted and halts for a human; bare lyx config with no TTY saves an empty layer
entries.body:
Two small bugs in one run, bundled on the operator's word (2026-10-15) to save a run's overhead, though they touch different packages.

# Part 1: begin-batch refusal route (issue #625, webster and loom)

## What happened

A task's run passed Plan-Bouncer (done) and Batchifier (done), then Webster's `lyx webster begin-batch 17` refused with `plan_drifted`.
The blocking finding was `delete-before-reference/18-retired-builders-delete[blocking]`: a card deletes a symbol that a later card still references in its Edit code.
`begin-batch 17` was refused twice with the identical finding, and the run halted `blocked` at Webster with anomaly `escalation-to-human`.

## Correction (orch, 2026-10-15)

In `overview-seats` the plan was not malformed: the reference was a temporary parity test that card 12's batch added after Plan-Write, inside a region card 18 itself rewrites, so the finding was a false positive of the check, fixed by `delete-order-own-edit` (landed 2026-10-14).

## What to do

- The refusal is labelled `plan_drifted` even when the plan did not drift from the tree but was malformed at authoring: distinguish the two in the refusal's classification, so the label names the right cause.
- A real `delete-before-reference` refusal at `begin-batch` has no route back to a plan-editing agent and halts for a human, though its text already names the way forward (move the delete to a later card, `lyx webster rebaseline --card NN`, then `begin-batch` again).
  Route it to a plan-fix step, or let Webster or the driver take that way, instead of halting.
- Consider running the `delete-before-reference` check at Plan-Bouncer or Batchifier time, so an ordering defect is fixed by the plan reviewers.

Provenance: task `overview-seats`.

# Part 2: bare `lyx config <module>` writes an empty layer (issue #632, config)

Seen (2026-10-15): a Discussion-Write agent in pair `webster-pack-end-of-prompt` ran `lyx config webster` with no arguments, expecting a read.
It replied `edited and synced _lyx/config/webster.yaml` and left a 0-byte `_lyx/config/webster.yaml` in the pair's worktree layer (behind the weft symlink, so `git status` shows nothing).
The bare form opens an editor; with no interactive terminal the editor exits at once and lyx saves the empty buffer as the layer.

Workaround: the orch never runs `lyx config` without `--set` or `--print`.

Expected: with no TTY, a bare `lyx config <module>` refuses (or prints) and never writes; an empty editor result is never saved over a layer.

entries.title: The arbiter in shed for every shed run, batten included
entries.brief: The batten Go driver has a tackler but no arbiter; move the arbiter and its keys into shed beside the tackler
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-15, after `shed-tackler` landed)

The Go driver in `internal/sheddriver` has an optional `Arbiter` seam.
Loom and darn fill it (`internal/loomcli/drivewiring.go`, `ArbiterSeam`), so their stop chain is: rule table, then the tackler (`haiku`), then the arbiter (`opus[high]`), then the orch.
Batten's own lifecycle run fills only the tackler (`internal/battencli/drive.go`, `sheddriver.Deps` has no `Arbiter`), so a stop the tackler escalates goes straight to the orch.
The arbiter's keys (`arbiter`, `arbiter_timeout_min`, `arbiter_max_spawns`) sit in `loom.yaml`, while the tackler's defaults moved to `shed.yaml`.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-15)

The stop chain should be the same for every shed run: if loom and darn have an arbiter, batten should have one too.
The arbiter is there to take load off the orch.

This matches the operator's 2026-10-14 principle that anything every FSM needs belongs in shed, with shed defaults a module's config overrides.

## Why batten has none: a recorded scope call in `shed-tackler`

`shed-tackler`'s decision record (records repo, commit `d921290f1`, `_lyx/discussion/decision-record.md`) put it out of scope on purpose:

- "The arbiter stays loom's code and config (`lyx loom arbiter`, `loomengine` arbiter settings); the driver reaches it only through a seam."
- "Arbiter: optional. Loom and darn wire `lyx loom arbiter`'s in-process path as today. Batten wires none; with no arbiter, a stop the rule table sends to the arbiter hands back, and a tackler `escalate` hands back with its case brief named in the hand-back notice."
- "Batten arms the `--until-stop` loop (`Spec.Loop`) without the agent idle watchdog, ... and without an arbiter attempt hook."

So the shared `sheddriver` code is the same, but the arbiter is an optional seam each recipe fills, and its implementation (`internal/loomcli/arbiter.go`, `internal/loomengine/arbiter.go`, `internal/arbiterstop`) is still loom's.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-15): per repo

The driver kind, and the stop chain's settings with it, must be settable per repo, including a worktree's local config layer.
Today `shed.yaml` already takes `driver_kind` and the tackler keys in the `default`, `worktree` and `local` layers (`lyx config shed --layer ...`), with `loom.yaml`, `darn.yaml` and `batten.yaml` as module overrides.
The arbiter's keys must work the same way once they move into `shed.yaml`.

## Idea

- Move the arbiter into shed beside the tackler: its seam wired for every shed-driven recipe, batten included, and its keys in `shed.yaml` with per-module overrides, as `driver_kind` and the tackler keys already are.
- Give batten an arbiter stencil or a recipe line that describes batten's rows (Worktree-Create, Run-Shed, Land, Worktree-Teardown and the rest), so the arbiter can judge a batten stop.

entries.title: Plan cards name added tests by Create handle, never a plain test-file path
entries.brief: Drop the Edit exception for a test file the card only adds tests to; the Create plan handle carries the file
entries.body:
## Seen

`contracts/stencils/loom/loom-template-plan.md` lets a card's `**Edit:**` list a plain test-file path "for a test file the card adds tests to without changing an existing member".
The same stencil already makes each new test function in an existing file a `**Create:**` declaration with a `plan:` handle, so the plain path only repeats where those new tests go.
No recorded reason for keeping both was found; the rule came in with `78a2b1f14` and was tightened in `c279a38ba`.
The 2026-10-15 pack audit (`.scratch/glyph-audit-3/`, to be committed under `docs/research/`) found that edits to files with no pack span were mostly md, yaml and test files, which this exception and the non-Go exception allow.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-15)

Test files should not be an exception to glyph references.

## Idea

- Drop the plain test-file path from `**Edit:**`: a card that adds tests to an existing file lists them only as `**Create:**` declarations with `plan:` handles, and the declaration carries the file.
- Have the plan gate refuse a plain `_test.go` path under `**Edit:**`, naming the way forward, and update `loom-plan-spec.md` and the stencil together.
- Check that Webster's kick-start pack and the fork prompt still tell the fork which file the new tests go in.

entries.title: Kick-start pack per card, read when the card starts
entries.brief: Forks read about a quarter of a batch-wide pack; hand each card its own pack as everything it needs to begin
entries.body:
## Seen

The 2026-10-15 pack audit (`.scratch/glyph-audit-3/`, to be committed under `docs/research/`) measured 24 Webster forks on the pack-file layout (`1e39afc10`).
Every fork opened the pack file in turn 2, but the median fork reached only about a quarter of its listed spans before its first edit, and only 7 of 24 read in parallel in their first work turn (52% under the earlier read-all-first layout).
A batch pack holds on average about 37 spans per fork, so "read every card and every span first" (`793c6a8ee`, today's `webster-fragment-locate-pack.md`) asks a fork to front-load a whole batch's code.
The pack entries were correct at batch start: 801 of 823 checked spans exact, 22 declaration-only, none stale or wrong.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-15)

Give the pack per card instead of per batch.
The batch gets one general instruction.
Each card then says: read this card's kick-start pack first; it is, to begin with, everything you need for this card.

## Idea

- Today's pack is one file per batch, `<batch>-pack.md`, already sectioned under each card's path; only the instruction makes it batch-wide.
  The cheapest form is therefore a new fragment text behind the switch: "before card N's first edit, read card N's section of the pack in one parallel turn", with no change to the pack file.
  The heavier form splits the pack into one file per card and hands each to the fork when it starts that card.
- Replace the read-all-first instruction with a per-card one: before the card's first edit, read its whole pack in one parallel turn.
- Frame the card pack as complete for a start, so the fork reads further only when the card needs it.
- Combine with putting the span code itself into the pack (separate idea from the same audit), so a card's pack is one read.

## Trade-off raised by the operator (2026-10-15): all at once lets the fork plan the whole batch

For reading everything first: the fork sees how the cards interact, plans the batch in one go, and fetches in one parallel turn instead of many small ones.
Against it: forks did not do it in the audit; code read in turn 2 is carried and paid as cache reads in every later turn, also through cards that do not need it; and line numbers go stale after the first edit anyway.
Two variants to measure against today's layout behind the switch:

1. Overview first, code per card (the orch's recommendation): at batch start the fork gets every card's intent and glyph list, no code, to plan the batch; it reads a card's spans when it starts that card.
2. All at once as today, but with the span code inside the pack file, so it is one read instead of about 37 and gets done; the context is as heavy as today's intended read.
- Keep the layout behind the `webster.yaml` switch, as `kickstart_pack_file` is today, so it can be measured against the current layout with the audit scripts.
- History: `113593990` had a per-card pack inline without a read rule (arm `mid` in the 2026-10-13 audit, 9 forks); this differs in giving each card its pack when that card starts.
